title: Unstressed о and а sound like “a” or “uh”
body: О keeps its “o” sound only when stressed. Right before the stress, and at the start of a word, о and а are a short “a”; in other unstressed syllables they are weaker still, like the “a” in “sofa”.

title: A consonant before е, ё, и, ю, я or ь is soft
body: Soft means said with the middle of the tongue raised toward the roof of the mouth, as if a tiny “y” followed, like the “n” in British “new”. It changes meaning: брат is “brother”, брать “to take”. In the respellings, “y” or ' marks a soft consonant.

title: Every word has one stressed syllable, and it is not marked
body: One syllable in each word is said louder and longer; the others are weak and short. Our texts do not mark it, it can fall on any syllable, and it can move between forms of one word (рука́, but ру́ку). Learn the stress with each word.

title: к, м, т look and sound like English k, m, t
body: Said as in English, but к and т without the puff of air, like the “k” in “skin” and the “t” in “stop”. т is made with the tongue touching the back of the top teeth.

title: о sounds like “o” in “or” when stressed
body: A short, rounded “o”, never the “oh” glide of English “go”. Unstressed, it changes to “a” or “uh” (see that rule).

title: б, д, з, п, ф sound like English b, d, z, p, f
body: Said as in English, with п less breathy, like the “p” in “spin”. At the end of a word or before a voiceless consonant б, д, з turn into п, т, с (see devoicing).

title: а sounds like “a” in “father”
body: Open and clear when stressed. Unstressed it becomes a short “a” or a weak “uh” (see the rule on unstressed о and а).

title: е says “ye”, or “e” after a consonant it softens
body: At the start of a word or after a vowel, е is “ye” as in “yes”. After a consonant it softens that consonant and sounds like the “e” in “met”. After ж, ш, ц it is a plain “e”; unstressed, it becomes a short “i”.

title: и sounds like “ee” in “see”
body: Short and clear, and it softens the consonant before it. After ж, ш and ц it sounds like ы instead (see that rule).

title: н looks like English H but sounds like “n”
body: A plain “n”, made with the tongue against the back of the top teeth. Before е, ё, и, ю, я, ь it is soft, like the “ny” in “canyon”.

title: с looks like English C but always sounds like “s”
body: Always a hissing “s” as in “sun”, never “k” and never “z” between vowels. Before б, г, д, ж, з it becomes “z” (see voicing).

title: л is a dark “l”, or a light one when soft
body: Plain л is said with the back of the tongue raised, like the deep “l” in “full”, even before а, о, у. Before е, ё, и, ю, я or ь it is light, like the “l” in “leaf”.

title: р looks like English P but is a rolled “r”
body: Tap or trill the tip of the tongue behind the top teeth, as in Spanish or Scottish “r”. Before е, ё, и, ю, я, ь it is soft, with the tongue raised.

title: Unstressed е and я sound like a short “i”
body: Away from the stress, е and я lose their own vowel and become a short “i” as in “bit”, still softening the consonant before them. Unstressed а after ч and щ does the same. At the very end of a word, unstressed я is a weak “yuh”.

title: в looks like English B but sounds like “v”
body: A plain “v”. Before a voiceless consonant and at the end of a word it becomes “f” (всё is “fsyo”). It never makes the consonant before it voiced.

title: у looks like English y but sounds like “oo”
body: A short “oo” with rounded lips, as in “moon” but shorter; never “yoo” and never “uh”. Unstressed it stays “oo”-like, just weaker, like the “u” in “put”.

title: ь has no sound: it softens the consonant before it
body: The soft sign makes the consonant before it soft (день, мать). Before е, ё, и, ю, я it also adds a full “y”: семья́ is “sim-YA”. After ж, ш, ч, щ it changes nothing in sound.

title: я says “ya”, or softens a consonant and says “a”
body: At the start of a word, after a vowel, or after ь and ъ, я is “ya” as in “yard”. After a consonant it softens that consonant and adds “a”. Unstressed, it becomes a short “i”.

title: ы is a deep “i” with the tongue pulled back
body: No exact English match: say the “i” of “bit”, then pull the tongue back without rounding the lips. The consonant before ы is always hard: compare бы (“bih”) with би (“bee”).

title: г is a hard “g” as in “go”
body: Always hard, never “j” as in “gem”, even before е and и. Two exceptions have their own rules: the endings -ого/-его (“v”), and г before к or ч (“kh”).

title: ч sounds like “ch” in “cheese”
body: Always soft, with the tongue raised, so а after it is never a hard “a”. In что, чтобы, конечно and скучно it says “sh” (see that rule).

title: й is a short “y” as in “boy”
body: It is never a vowel on its own: it glides off the vowel before it. ай sounds like “eye”, ой like “oy” in “boy”, ей like “ay” in “day”.

title: One-letter prepositions в, с, к join the next word
body: They have no vowel, so they are said as the first sound of the next word, and they take on its voicing: в before a voiceless consonant is “f”, с before a voiced one is “z”.

title: After ж, ш, ц, the letter и sounds like ы and е like э
body: These three consonants are always hard, so the vowel after them is said the hard way: жи, ши, ци sound like “zhih”, “shih”, “tsih”, and же, ше, це have no “y”.

title: ж sounds like the “s” in “measure”
body: The voiced partner of ш, always hard: и after it sounds like ы. At the end of a word or before a voiceless consonant it becomes “sh”.

title: Neighbouring consonants match in voice
body: Before a voiceless consonant (к, п, с, т, ф, х, ц, ч, ш, щ), the letters б, в, г, д, ж, з turn into п, ф, к, т, ш, с. Before б, г, д, ж, з (but not в) a voiceless consonant becomes voiced: с turns into “z”, к into “g”, т into “d”.

title: ш sounds like a hard “sh”
body: Like English “sh”, but with the tongue pulled back and the lips not rounded, which gives a deeper sound. It is always hard: и after it sounds like ы.

title: х sounds like the “ch” in Scottish “loch”
body: A rough, breathy sound from the back of the mouth, never silent and never “ks”. Before е and и it is softer, closer to the “h” in “huge”.

title: б, в, г, д, ж, з at the end of a word lose their voice
body: At the end of a word they are said as п, ф, к, т, ш, с: хлеб is “khlyep”, год is “got”. The spelling does not change.

title: ю says “yu”, or softens a consonant and says “u”
body: At the start of a word, after a vowel, or after ь and ъ, ю is “yoo” as in “you”. After a consonant it softens that consonant and adds “oo”.

title: ц sounds like “ts” in “cats”
body: One quick sound, even at the start of a word. It is always hard: и after it sounds like ы, and е like э.

title: ё is always stressed and says “yo”
body: Our texts print ё with its dots, so it shows you the stress. At the start of a word or after a vowel it is “yo”; after a consonant it softens it and adds “o”. After ж, ш, ч, щ it is just “o”.

title: Double consonants are held a little longer
body: Between vowels, especially right after the stress, a double letter is held longer, like the “nn” in “unnamed”. Next to another consonant, at the end of a word, or in many longer words it is said as a single sound.

title: ч sounds like “sh” in что, чтобы, конечно, скучно
body: In these common words ч is said “sh”: что is “shto”. Elsewhere, including ничего and most words with чн, it stays “ch”.

title: г in the endings -ого and -его sounds like “v”
body: In these adjective and pronoun endings, and in сегодня, г is said “v”. Where -ого is part of the word itself, not an ending, г stays “g”: много, дорого.

title: э sounds like “e” in “met”
body: A plain “e” with no “y” in front, and it does not soften the consonant before it. It is used mainly at the start of words and in borrowed words.

title: щ is a long soft “sh”
body: Hold a soft “sh” a little longer, with the middle of the tongue raised, like “sh sh” in “fresh sheets” run together. Older books describe it as “shch”. It is always soft.

title: -тся and -ться at the end of a verb sound like “tsuh”
body: Both spellings sound the same: a long “ts” followed by a weak “uh”. The soft sign makes no difference here.

title: т and д merge with a following ц, ч or ск
body: тц and дц are one long “ts”, тч and дч one long “ch”, and тск, дск are said “tsk”. So два́дцать is “DVA-tsuht'”.

title: Some consonants in clusters are silent
body: In a few clusters one letter drops out: the first в in вств, л in лнц, д in рдц and здн, т in стн and стл. So здра́вствуйте is “ZDRAST-vuy-tye” and со́лнце is “SON-tsuh”.

title: сч, зч and жч sound like щ
body: These pairs merge into one long soft “sh”, exactly like щ: счёт is “shshot”.

title: In some borrowed words е does not soften the consonant
body: In a number of borrowed words the consonant before е stays hard and е sounds like э: кафе́ is “ka-FEH”, not “ka-FYE”. Common ones are кафе, интернет, отель, тест, модель, компьютер, менеджер.

title: ъ has no sound: it splits a consonant from a “y” sound
body: The hard sign appears after a prefix, before е, ё, ю, я. It keeps the consonant before it hard and makes the vowel start with a clear “y”: подъе́зд is “pad-YEST”.

title: зж, жж, сш and зш merge into a long “zh” or “sh”
body: The first consonant takes on the sound of the second, and the two are said as one long sound: по́зже is “POZH-zhih”.

title: г before к or ч sounds like “kh”
body: In легко, мягкий and related words, г is said like х, the rough “ch” of Scottish “loch”.
